posts.author: MichaelH
posts.content_md:
After much:

1. experimentation.

2. mount tweaking.

3. video taping.

4. repeating of 1-3 many times.

I found a 90% solution. I don't remember where I first heard about this but I believe someone at one of the PCG meetings mentioned leaning metal rods against the plate holder to dampen ringing in the holder. That turned out to take care of most of the problem I had in the holder and one of my mirror mounts. I could tap my plate holder and it would ring for 3-4 seconds. Now the effects from tapping the holder (not quite a ring) is down to about a second. I've got some video that I'll post once I've captured it to disk.

I've also found that putting a heavy magnet at the side-top of the mirror mount does much the same thing as leaning a heavy metal rod against it.

posts.author: MichaelH
posts.content_md:
After much more testing (although not as much as I'd like, silly work-thing kept getting in the way) I've determined that life in my lab is much better without the inner tubes.

The same day last week that I found evidence of this I later listened to the interview between Frank and Ken Dunkley where Ken mentions that in his testing ages ago he found the same thing. Inner tubes make table stability worse.

This weekend I finished building up my table legs and found that 10" of a combination of bubble-wrap and carpet does a great job of damping vibrations and I no longer have the problem of the table "breathing" when the ambient air pressure changes.

This is the classic theory of table design. Make the table as massive as possible and lower the fundemental resonance to around 6hz then design isolation legs for that frequency. This works well! For those of use that rent it is a difficult solution as a 2 ton table is not very protable. 

Sand was the next solution. Now people are afraid of the dust. I don't know why, there are beautiful holograms made on sand tables. I choose to go a different rout. Design a table that is very stiff and light. I have not done thorough testing of my table so I don't yet know if it was the best solution.

posts.author: Colin Kaminski
posts.content_md:
> **Hans:** So, I was wondering if due to the fact that the A1-32-5 being less stiff, will there still be a long settling time due to the table bending and sagging more when the material is less stiff? What I mean to say is: Will a softer table take a significantly longer time to reach it's final bending state after components are placed on it than a stiffer table?

That has not been my experience. I have found on tables that are less stiff I have more beam allignment problems as I move optics around slowing the process of changing from one setup to another. Also they are significantly more prone to random vibrations. With a stiff table there is very little energy available to make a less than perfect optic or film mount vibrate. Life is simply easier with a stiffer table. When I did the math I liked the steel honeycomb best but i settled for alluminum as that was what was available surplus.

I think I would look at the numbers of doing a Duocell (SP) foam core as well. Also vertical grain balsa wood's numbers ran pretty good. Aluminum foam's numbers ran great but I could not find any even though I live 45 minutes from a very large manufacturer. When I contacted them and explaiined my project they said they could not do it but asked if I wanted to come in for a job interview. It seems they were looking for a person that could babysit special projects through the plant. I declined the interview.

There is a lot of foams being used for homebuilt aircraft these days. Look into the latest and greatest as it will have very good numbers compared to honeycomb. The foams are heavy as the 8# per ft^3 are the range of numbers that start to become usefull.

So the numbers I have from years ago:

Blue Foam Shear Modulus (lb/ft^2) - 96336

Duocel Shear Modulus (lb/ft^2) - 633600

Vertical Balsa Wood Shear Modulus (lb/ft^2) - 2001600

And I ran the numbers on three different Honeycombs. As you can see balsa was very good but very labor intensive to make. I never did any humidity measurements to see if balso would work but I suspect it would be fine if it was sealed.

posts.content_md:
> Hi Hans, the hexcel I ended up with was "CR III 5052 & 5056 Corrosion Resistant Specification Grade Aluminum 1/8 4.5lb core" It's all covered in the PDF paper I linked to previously.

Thank you Michael. 

So I now know I must be doing something wrong when I try to get the numbers from the datasheet. The specs for the 1/8-5056-.001 material are in the datasheet as follows:

- Nominal Density: 4.5pcf

- Compressive Modulus: K = 185000psi = 2.664 * 10^7 lbs/feet^2

- Plate Shear Modulus (L direction): Gl = 70000psi = 1.008*10^7 lbs/feet^2

- Plate Shear Modulus (W direction):Gw = 28000psi = 0.4032*10^7 lbs/feet^2

Young's Modulus is not specified in the datasheet. But there is a way to calculate it.

============================================================

To get Young's modulus from these numbers (using the Shear Modulus in the L direction): 

Poisson's Ratio = v = (3 * K - 2 * Gl) / (2 * Gl + 6 * K) = 0.332

Young's Modulus = E = 3 * K * (1 - 2 * v) = 2.685*10^7 lbs/feet^2

============================================================

Here's where I think I do something wrong because the value that you use and the one that is used in the LEOT tutorial for Young's Modulus is 200 times bigger than the one I just derived with the help of Poisson's ratio.

If I use the derived number for Young's Modulus in the formula for table deflection (instead of the one you and the LEOT tutorial use), I get a much bigger deflection of the table with a 100lbs weight placed on it:

-- Deflection = 0.3mm

-- Deflection in Wavelengths (at 633nm) = 483

posts.author: Colin Kaminski
posts.content_md:
![StiffenssEq.gif](https://holographyforum.org/forum/download/file.php?id=6005)

where: P = Force exerted by the point load (in lbs)

L = Length of the panel (in ft)

b = Width of the panel (in ft)

H = Thickness of the pane (in ft)

T = Thickness of the skins (in ft)

E = Young’s modulus for the skin material (in lb/ft2)

G = Shear modulus for the core (in lb/ft2)

With these units, the deflection will come out in ft.

So the only Young's modulus you need is the skin material itself not the core.
